OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
For which number theoretic functions $f$ is it true that, for any $F(n)$ such that $F(n)/f(n)\to 0$ for almost all $n$, there are infinitely many $x$ such that\[\frac{\#\{ n\in \mathbb{N} : n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}\to \infty?\]
#122: [Er97,p.155][Er97e,p.533][EPS97]
number theory
In [Er97] Erdős is only considering number theoretic functions which grow 'slowly' (i.e. slower than $(\log n)^{1-c}$ for some $c>0$). 
This is considered by Erdős, Pomerance, and Sárközy [EPS97], who prove in particular that if $\omega(n)$ counts the number of distinct prime divisors of $n$, then for all large $x$ there are intervals $I,J\subset [1,x]$ of width\[\lvert I\rvert\asymp \left(\frac{\log x}{\log\log x}\right)^{1/2}\]and\[\lvert J\rvert \asymp (\log\log x)^{1/2}\]such that if $n\in I$ then $n+\omega(n)\in J$. (Note the normal order of $\omega$ is $\log\log x$, and hence $(\log\log n)^{1/2}/\omega(n)\to 0$ for almost all $n$.) 
In [Er97] and [Er97e] Erdős reports that he, Pomerance, and Sárkzözy can prove the more general claim above for $f$ being $\tau(n)$, the divisor function, or $\omega(n)$, and states it 'probably fails' for $\phi(n)$ or $\sigma(n)$. 
Additional thanks to: Stijn Cambie and Wouter van Doorn

 If the sites wording is taken literally with \(x\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}\) and \(F\) positive and real-valued, the statement has a very elementary disproof.
For \(f:\mathbb{N}_{>0}\to\mathbb{N}_{>0}\), define\[
F(x)=\frac1x.
\]Then\[
0<\frac{F(x)}{f(x)}
=\frac{1}{xf(x)}
\le\frac1x\to0.
\]But for \(x\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}\),\[
n+f(n)\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}
\quad\text{and}\quad
(x,x+F(x))
=
\left(x,x+\frac1x\right)
\subseteq(x,x+1),
\]so\[
\operatorname{card}\{n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}:n+f(n)\in(x,x+F(x))\}=0.
\]I would guess this is not what Erdos wanted though. The historical problem likely has more to it.

 I think I made a counterexample to this.
A short counterexample to the current online formulation of Problem #122.
Let\[
R(x):=\frac{\#\{n\in \mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}.
\]I am only addressing the current online version of problem#122 as written above. I am not claiming to have resolved the historical original problem behind Problem #122.
Assume throughout that\[
f:\mathbb{N}\to [0,\infty).
\]I claim that for every such nonnegative function \(f\), there exists an integer-valued function \(F:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\) such that\[
\frac{f(n)}{F(n)}\to 0 \qquad (n\to\infty),
\]but at the same time\[
R(x)<2 \qquad \text{for every }x\in\mathbb{N}.
\]This shows that the current online formulation is false under any natural interpretation in which the displayed ratio is supposed to become arbitrarily large as \(x\) varies.
Indeed, define\[
F(n):=1+\left\lceil n^2+f(n)^2\right\rceil \qquad (n\in\mathbb{N}).
\]Then \(F(n)\in\mathbb{N}\) and\[
F(n)\ge 1+n^2+f(n)^2.
\]Hence\[
0\le \frac{f(n)}{F(n)}\le \frac{f(n)}{n^2+f(n)^2}.
\]By the elementary inequality\[
n^2+f(n)^2\ge 2nf(n),
\]we get\[
\frac{f(n)}{n^2+f(n)^2}\le \frac{1}{2n}.
\]Therefore\[
0\le \frac{f(n)}{F(n)}\le \frac{1}{2n}\to 0.
\]Now fix \(x\in\mathbb{N}\), and let\[
A_x:=\{n\in\mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}.
\]If \(n\in A_x\), then\[
n+f(n)<x+F(x).
\]Since \(f(n)\ge 0\), it follows that\[
n\le n+f(n)<x+F(x).
\]Thus every element of \(A_x\) is a natural number strictly smaller than \(x+F(x)\). Consequently,\[
\#A_x\le x+F(x).
\]Dividing by \(F(x)\), we obtain\[
R(x)=\frac{\#A_x}{F(x)}\le 1+\frac{x}{F(x)}.
\]But\[
F(x)\ge 1+x^2+f(x)^2\ge 1+x^2,
\]so\[
R(x)\le 1+\frac{x}{x^2+1}<2.
\]Hence\[
\frac{\#\{n\in \mathbb{N}: n+f(n)\in (x,x+F(x))\}}{F(x)}<2
\qquad \text{for all }x\in\mathbb{N}.
\]

 Yes, I think this is the correct interpretation: in [Er97] and [Er97e] there was just a typo (reproduced here) writing $f/F$ where they meant $F/f$. (Although this is more than just a typo in [Er97], since he explicitly states that the width of the interval (here denoted $F(x)$) 'tends to infinity faster than does [the normal order of $f$]'.
Further evidence is looking at what [EPS97] actually prove - they don't state it as a main result, but their methods prove (implicitly) that there is an interval $I\subset [1,O(x)]$ of width\[\asymp \left(\frac{\log x}{\log\log x}\right)^{1/2}\]such that if $n\in I$ then $n+\omega(n)$ is in $J$, where $J$ is an interval of width $O((\log\log x)^{1/2})$ (and the normal order of $\omega$ is $\log\log x$). 
The motivation for this sort of problem is to generalise results like 'there are infinitely many $m$ such that $n+\omega(n)=m$ has many solutions'. In this formulation we replace $m$ with a short interval instead, and want many values of $n+\omega(n)$ in this interval. 
As is the case with many of the problems stated in [Er97] and [Er97e] there are definitely some errors here; also in the description of the results obtained (which don't really appear in [EPS97]). I'll email Pomerance to see if he can clarify and/or provide other references.
